passage: In the school library, Gautam stared at the list: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The exam was tomorrow. He tried saying them again and again. The teacher, Vidya, looked up from her desk. "What would help you?" Gautam frowned, then his eyes lit up. "The first letters! M, V, E, M, J, S, U, N. Let me make a sentence. My Very Elegant Monkey Jumps Skipping Under Nets." He laughed. "A monkey with a skipping rope! Now I can see it." He wrote it in the corner of his notebook and repeated it once, then closed his eyes and recited the planets in order without a mistake.

qa.q: What silly sentence did Gautam make?
qa.a: Gautam made the sentence 'My Very Elegant Monkey Jumps Skipping Under Nets.'

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when he made the sentence, and what did he think it would do?
qa.a: Gautam felt amused and excited; he laughed at the monkey with a skipping rope and thought the funny picture would help him see and recall the planets in order.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Gautam use for the planets, and why?
qa.a: Gautam could draw the planets in a row or say them in rhythm as a chant. A picture or a rhythm gives another route to the order.

qa.q: How might Vidya see Gautam's idea?
qa.a: Vidya asked a simple question and let Gautam find the answer, so Vidya probably feels pleased to see the boy solve the problem alone.

grounding: A boy makes a silly sentence from the first letters of the planets, and the story links the separate items so they are recalled in order.

passage: Dhruv sits next to me, Amandeep, in Class 5, and on Tuesday he was muttering during break. "My. Very. Eager. Monkey. Just. Sat. Upon. Nani." I asked if he'd gone mad. He showed me his rough page. Down one side: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Across: the silly sentence. "Each first letter is a planet," he said. "I can't remember eight names in a row. But I can see a monkey sitting on Nani. The monkey pulls the next word along." He was grinning like he'd found a secret door. On Friday Sharma sir asked the class for the planets in order. Dhruv's hand went up first, and I saw his lips move, just a little, before he answered.

qa.q: What sentence did Dhruv mutter during break?
qa.a: He muttered "My. Very. Eager. Monkey. Just. Sat. Upon. Nani."

qa.q: What does Dhruv's grin suggest he was feeling when he explained the sentence?
qa.a: He seemed delighted and proud, as if he had found a secret way into something hard.

qa.q: What else could Dhruv use if he needs to remember a list that is not in order?
qa.a: He could draw a quick picture for each item, because images stick even when order does not matter.

qa.q: How does Dhruv's trick look to Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep first thinks Dhruv has gone mad, then sees the trick work in class, so it probably looks clever and worth copying.

grounding: It shows a boy making a silly sentence from the planets' first letters so the items link together in order.

passage:
Monday: Science test on Thursday, and Zubin kept mixing up Uranus and Neptune. "Eight planets in order is too many," he told Joseph on the bus.
Tuesday: At home he wrote the first letters on a card. M, V, E, M, J, S, U, N. He stared, then laughed. "Mummy Visits Every Market, Just Selling Umbrellas Now." He could picture it: Mummy with a pile of umbrellas in the rain. "Umbrellas comes before Now," he said to himself, "so Uranus comes before Neptune. Done."
Thursday: Joseph nudged him before the paper. "Say it." Zubin whispered the umbrella sentence, then wrote all eight planets in the right order without crossing anything out.

qa.q: Which two planets did Zubin keep mixing up?
qa.a: He kept mixing up Uranus and Neptune.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when he came up with the umbrella sentence?
qa.a: He felt amused and relieved, laughing because the picture made the order easy to hold.

qa.q: What else could Zubin try to check he really knows the order?
qa.a: He could say the planets backwards from the sentence, because testing himself shows whether the link holds without the card.

qa.q: How does Zubin's trick look to Joseph?
qa.a: Joseph trusts it enough to ask him to say it before the paper, so it looks useful and maybe fun to him.

grounding: It shows a boy turning the planets' first letters into a funny sentence that links them in order.
